kurz: Contracts relating to a future date whose value depends entirely on another variable, and why with them every gain corresponds to a loss on the other side.

bloecke.md:
A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from another variable. The name comes from the Latin *derivare*, to derive. This variable is called the underlying. It can be a share, an index, an interest rate, an exchange rate, a barrel of oil, a tonne of wheat, an emission allowance or the number of frost days in a district. The type of underlying does not matter. However, its value must be observable at the agreed time and must be determinable in a way that neither side can dispute.

Derivatives differ fundamentally from the investments covered in the previous modules. A buyer of shares takes over an existing stake from the previous holder, and the number of shares does not change as a result. Buyers of an option or a futures contract, by contrast, enter into a new contract with the other side that did not exist before. Derivatives are agreements whose number is not limited. They come into being when two parties conclude them and disappear when these parties close them out. This is why the outstanding volume of derivatives on an underlying can exceed the available quantity of that underlying many times over without this indicating dubious business.
A derivative does not create value. When used for hedging, it shifts an existing risk from someone who does not want to bear it to someone who takes it on in return for payment.

## The forward transaction as the basic form

Every market transaction has two points in time: conclusion and settlement. In a spot transaction, the two practically coincide. A share bought today is in the securities account two banking days later, and the purchase price has been debited. In a forward transaction (Termingeschäft), conclusion and settlement are separated in time. Price, quantity and date are set today; delivery and payment follow later. This time gap is what makes the forward transaction a derivative.

Every contract must therefore contain four details: the underlying, the contract size, the settlement date and the price agreed today. If one of them is missing, it is merely a declaration of intent.

Forward transactions can be divided into two groups, and this distinction is the most important in the whole module. In an **unconditional** forward transaction (future, forward, swap), both sides are bound. Neither side has a choice; both must perform. Gain and loss are therefore mirror images and open in both directions. In a **conditional** forward transaction, the option, one side has a right and the other an obligation. The buyer may demand performance, and the seller must then provide it. For this right to choose, the buyer pays a price, the premium.

bloecke.md:
A swap is a series of forward transactions with staggered maturities. Two parties exchange payment streams over a period of years, typically a fixed interest rate for a floating one. Measured by notional volume, interest rate swaps are by far the largest category of derivatives in the world. This is not due to speculation by banks. Swaps are used to give practically every large portfolio of loans and bonds the desired fixed-rate period.

## Exchange trading, OTC trading and securitised derivatives

On a **derivatives exchange** such as Eurex, contracts are standardised, with fixed strike prices, expiry dates and contract sizes. A central counterparty, the clearing house, steps in between buyer and seller. It becomes the seller to every buyer and vice versa, demands collateral from both sides and settles daily. Counterparty default risk therefore still exists, but it is concentrated at the clearing house, covered by collateral and monitored. Eurex lists over 700 equity options and over 800 single stock futures (as of October 2026).

In **over-the-counter trading** (OTC), contracts are concluded that are meant to be individually tailored, for example a currency forward for $8.4 million maturing on 14 March. No clearing house is interposed here; each side depends on the creditworthiness of its counterparty. After the financial crisis, EU Regulation 648/2012 (EMIR) made central clearing, collateralisation and reporting obligations mandatory for large parts of this market.

For private investors, there is a third route, **securitised derivatives**. These include warrants, certificates and knock-outs. Legally, they are bearer bonds (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen) issued by a bank. For tax purposes, they do not count as forward transactions, but the Securities Trading Act (WpHG) classifies warrants as financial forward transactions (Finanztermingeschäfte, Section 99 WpHG). The investor trades with the issuer as counterparty, and the issuer also sets the price.

bloecke.unter: On the derivatives exchange, the clearing house enters into every contract and demands collateral daily; over the counter, counterparty default risk remains between the two contracting parties.

bloecke.md:
## Market participants and their motives

Participants with three different motives trade on the derivatives market. All three are needed, because a market in which only one of them existed would have no prices.

The **hedger** bears a risk from their business that they want to pass on. In May, a farmer knows their costs but not the wheat price in August. A machinery manufacturer calculates in euros and will receive dollars in six months. A pension fund has liabilities with fixed maturities and investments with different maturities. For these participants, the derivative is a planning tool.

The **speculator** has no such underlying business. They take on the risk voluntarily because they expect to be paid for it. The word is often used disparagingly, but without speculators the hedger would find no counterparty, or only at a very poor price. The liquidity that ensures a narrow gap between bid and ask prices comes mainly from participants who never intend to take delivery of the goods.

The **arbitrageur** looks for prices that are inconsistent with each other. The forward price of a storable commodity is derived from the spot price plus financing and storage costs and is therefore not a forecast. If it is higher, the arbitrageur buys the commodity, stores it and at the same time sells it forward. Such risk-free transactions pay off until the difference has disappeared. Arbitrage keeps the spot and forward markets linked to each other.

A company delivers in March and receives $10 million in September. The exchange rate is 1.10 dollars per euro, and the order was costed with revenue of €9.09 million. Through a currency forward, the company sells the $10 million for September at a fixed rate of 1.10.

If the euro is at 1.20 in September, the dollars would bring in only €8.33 million on the spot market. In this case, the forward transaction brings in around €758,000 more. If it is at 1.00, the revenue would have been €10.00 million, and the forward transaction costs just over €909,000.

The hedge therefore gives the company fixed revenue, but no additional profit. In about half of all cases it costs money; that is the price of planning certainty. (The actual forward rate differs from the spot rate by the interest rate differential between the euro and the dollar; it has been left out of the example.)

bloecke.titel: Euro revenue from $10 million, with and without a currency forward
bloecke.unter: Without a hedge, the euro revenue depends on the exchange rate; with the forward transaction, it is the same at every rate. Illustrative calculation without interest rate differential and costs.

bloecke.md:
## Derivatives as a zero-sum game

A share can perform well for everyone involved at the same time. The company generates profits, pays dividends and invests. Its value grows, and every shareholder shares in this without anyone else having to give anything up. A derivative contract, by contrast, generates nothing, because there are no employees, no machines and no revenue behind it. What one side gains, the other loses in the same contract, at the same time and by the same amount.

This statement is meant in an accounting sense, not a moral one, and has two consequences. First, the derivatives market lacks the growth in value from which everyone benefits on the stock market. There, an investor still makes money even with a selection that is poor on average, because the companies in the background generate earnings. On the derivatives market, by contrast, every euro gained has to be taken from another participant. Second, after costs the zero-sum game becomes a negative-sum game. Spread, order fees and exchange fees flow out of the system, as does the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) on the winning side, insofar as the loser cannot offset their loss against other capital income. Gains from forward transactions are capital income under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act). They are taxed at 25% plus solidarity surcharge (Section 32d(1) EStG), making 26.375% in total.

bloecke.titel: Result for both sides after costs and tax
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a €1,000 gain that changes hands, an order fee of €12 per side and a winner who has already used up their saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) and pays tax on €988 after deducting their fee. It is assumed that the loser cannot offset their loss of €1,012. If they can offset it against other taxable capital income, they save around €267 in tax, and a loss of around €18 remains for both sides together.

bloecke.md:
The zero sum only concerns the amounts of money; both sides can still benefit. A farmer who fixes their wheat price in May has an advantage even if, on paper, they receive less in August than they would have without the hedge. They were able to plan their costs, service loans and buy fertiliser without having to follow the market price every day. The other side took on the risk and was paid for it. Both are better off after the transaction than before, even though not a single additional euro has been created.

This is what distinguishes a derivative used for hedging from a derivative used as a bet. For hedging, it offsets a risk that the user already bears. As a bet, it creates a risk that did not exist before. The contract is the same in both cases. The difference lies solely in what else is on the balance sheet or in the portfolio.

A Eurex DAX future (FDAX) is specified at €25 per index point. With the DAX at 20,000 points, a single contract corresponds to a notional value of €500,000. Only part of this has to be deposited as collateral. Investors who measure their leverage against the capital invested instead of the notional value systematically underestimate the size of their position.

In statistics, the same confusion occurs in the opposite direction. The reported notional volumes of derivatives markets are reference amounts and not sums that anyone could lose. The gross market value of outstanding contracts is far lower; for OTC derivatives at the end of 2025, it was just under 3% of the notional volume. With headlines about risks running into trillions, you should therefore first check which of the two figures is meant.

## History of derivatives

Derivatives seem like a modern invention, but they are very old. In the *Politics*, Aristotle tells of Thales of Miletus. On the basis of a harvest forecast, Thales secured the rights to use the olive presses in the area for little money and passed them on at a high price at harvest time. Aristotle cites this as an example of a monopoly and not of a derivative. The structure of the transaction, however, corresponds to that of a call, that is, a right without an obligation, acquired with an advance payment.

This pattern has repeated itself in the same form ever since. Wherever a commodity is perishable, the quantity fluctuates and the price is only known after the harvest, forward markets emerge, for example for rice in Osaka, tulip bulbs in Amsterdam and grain in Chicago. The only new elements are standardisation, central clearing and model-based valuation.

bloecke.unter: Each stage of development responds to the same problem: fixing a future price without having to trust the other side completely.

ereignisse.text: Rice merchants found the rice exchange, which the shogunate licenses in 1730. In the 18th century, organised forward trading in rice develops there, the first of its kind.
Grain merchants found an exchange at which harvest prices are fixed in advance. From 1865, the forwards become standardised futures.
The CBOE becomes the first trading venue to open trading in standardised equity options. In the same year, the valuation model by Black and Scholes is published.
On 26 January, fully electronic derivatives trading starts in Frankfurt, initially with options only and later with futures as well.
The DTB and the Swiss SOFFEX merge. Just over 248 million contracts are traded in the first financial year.
Default insurance on mortgage securities, traded over the counter, pushes the insurer AIG to the brink of insolvency.
EU Regulation 648/2012 requires central clearing for standardised OTC derivatives and reporting to a trade repository.

bloecke.md: Derivatives thus have a dual nature. The same instrument that allows an exporter to plan reliably turns a modest portfolio into a position with a six-figure notional value for a private investor without an underlying business. The instrument itself is neutral. Its effect depends on whether it is accompanied by a risk that it offsets or only by a view on the market.

mitnehmen: A derivative is a contract relating to a future date whose value depends entirely on another variable, the underlying.
Unconditional forward transactions bind both sides; conditional ones give one side a choice, for which the premium is paid.
Hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs need each other, because without someone to take on the risk, there would be no counterparty for the hedger.
On the derivatives market, every gain is the loss of a counterparty, and after costs and tax the combined result of all participants is negative.
The notional value of a contract is the reference amount for the calculation and is neither the capital invested nor the market value.

begriffe.text: Contract whose value is derived entirely from another variable, the underlying. It comes into being when two parties conclude the contract and does not represent ownership of an asset.
The reference variable of a derivative, for example a share, index, interest rate, exchange rate, commodity or any other variable whose value can be determined beyond dispute on the due date.

Also called a forward transaction: a transaction in which conclusion and settlement are separated in time. Unconditional forward transactions (future, forward, swap) bind both sides; conditional ones (option) give one side a choice.
Clearing house that enters into every contract for exchange-traded derivatives. It is the seller to every buyer and vice versa, calls in collateral and settles daily.
The value of the underlying to which a contract relates, for the FDAX, for example, index level × €25. It is neither the capital invested nor the market value of the contract.
